When night falls, the light from Cantine Burgz, Jackson Joseph’s restaurant, lights up the sidewalk like a lantern. In the afternoon, the brightness inside almost rivals daylight. Walking past the window, many passersby wave to the owner. “It’s like a fish tank in here. You see everything.”
Si c’est Jackson qu’on remarque derrière: Jackson may be the one people notice behind the window, but he is the one doing the observing. A lifelong resident, he has known only Montréal’s Sud-Ouest, and nothing escapes him.
À la fréquence à laquelle jeunes et moin: Judging by how often young and old alike wave at him as they go by, it’s easy to picture people lining up at the counter at mealtimes. You can conclude that the restaurant and its owner are well liked in the area. But behind his unshakeable pragmatism, he’s not the one who will tell you that.
À la Cantine Burgz, on savoure des plats: At Cantine Burgz, you can enjoy comforting Haitian dishes, prepared in the traditional way. Mr. Joseph has brought together two things he is particularly fond of: the cooking of his country of origin and this neighbourhood he holds dear. And while the recipe is traditional, the chicken here is halal. “I have friends who are part of the Muslim community. Out of respect for people of that faith, I do it,” says the restaurateur, who does not practise any religion. With summer approaching, he promises new items on the menu, including dishes to eat on the go.
L’idée d’ouvrir un comptoir lui est venu: The idea of opening a counter came to him during a visit from family from the United States. “I had cousins who came from Boston. They wanted to eat Haitian food and I realized we didn’t have any in this part of the city,” he says. Three years later, in the summer of 2020, the restaurant opened its doors on Charlevoix Street in Pointe-Saint-Charles.
« J’ai décidé que, malgré la pandémie, i: “I decided that, despite the pandemic, we had to keep going,” he recalls. The difficulties were many: labour and materials were hard to come by, physical distancing was the rule, and curfews followed one after another. Mr. Joseph estimates that the events and the climate created by the pandemic cost him significant revenue. But that did not stop him from moving forward.
Joseph avait été employé toute sa vie, m: Joseph had been an employee all his life, but the choice to become an entrepreneur came naturally. “I worked in the same place for 23 years. I realized that if I wasn’t at the top, I had trouble with authority,” says the man who describes himself as a free spirit. For Mr. Joseph, the most important thing is to be true to yourself. “We stay authentic, sometimes crazy in the eyes of some,” says the owner.
Certains ont d’ailleurs dû le trouver fo: Some, in fact, must have thought he was crazy to take on a project like this. “When you start a business, of course you have failures. But I don’t call them failures; it’s a learning process. Sometimes failure is essential and necessary to start over stronger,” he says, offering advice to those who might want to take the plunge. He then quotes Mandela on the subject: “I never lose. I either win or learn.”
Joseph n’avait donc aucune expérience en: Joseph therefore had no restaurant experience. “Honestly, I really learned on the job,” he confides. He decided, however, to put to use what he knows best: customer service. He considers it a particularly important field, and one where he sometimes notices shortcomings. “I’m not the one who does the cooking!” Mr. Joseph clarifies. “I worked in a sports centre. Customer service is something I have in me, something I’ve experienced, that I know well.”
Le service devient ainsi son <em>modus o: Service thus becomes his modus operandi. “A customer is a human being,” says Mr. Joseph. When the restaurant opened, customers felt a need to stay connected. “At the beginning of the pandemic, I knew I had a role to play, almost like providing psychological support,” he remembers. At the time, people had few opportunities to go out. So he lets visitors to the restaurant speak freely, or simply enjoy one another’s presence. He also feels the effect of such a welcome. “Telling someone you thought of them, or taking the time to tell them something, pulled me out of isolation,” he points out. Nearly three years later, he remains in the same spirit. “Every human being needs to be listened to. Listening is a beautiful thing. Talking is good, but listening is better.”
Aux dires du propriétaire, c’est le bouc: According to the owner, word of mouth is behind the restaurant’s success. As is well known, the restaurant business is a tough one when it comes to turnover. “I wanted organic growth. But that’s not enough, given the circumstances,” he says, wondering what comes next. Some neighbourhood residents come every week; others tell him they didn’t know the place existed when they stop in to take a look. Mr. Jackson estimates that the majority of his customers are not of Haitian origin. They are also, he believes, the most demanding customers.
Jackson Joseph vit dans ce quartier depu: Jackson Joseph has lived in this neighbourhood all his life. His parents settled here before he was born. “I thank my parents a lot for making that choice. Now, honestly, I can’t see myself living anywhere else. We’re close to everything. We have a jewel here, like the Lachine Canal. It’s a neighbourhood that’s vibrant, that’s very alive,” he explains. Mr. Jackson tells how his father, whom he describes as a visionary, saw the area’s full potential more than 40 years ago. “He told me back then, when I was very little: ‘These neighbourhoods are going to be unaffordable. People won’t be able to live there anymore,’” the entrepreneur recalls.
Ces quartiers, c’est la Petite-Bourgogne: These neighbourhoods are Little Burgundy and its surroundings, that is, the neighbouring areas whose boundaries are blurry for locals: Griffintown, Saint-Henri and Pointe-Saint-Charles, where Cantine Burgz is located.
Le nom du restaurant est un hommage à la: The restaurant’s name is a tribute to Little Burgundy, which its residents sometimes call “Burgundy.” Mr. Joseph had to resign himself to setting up his business on the other side of the Lachine Canal. “I tried everything to get a space. The reality is that right now, in Little Burgundy, commercial rent is exorbitant,” he laments.
Ce quartier, qui est historiquement ouvr: This historically working-class neighbourhood is the birthplace of jazz and of Montréal’s Black communities. It was originally the city’s multi-ethnic neighbourhood. Today, Little Burgundy is made up mainly of social housing. However, Notre-Dame Street, its main artery, has a large number of luxury businesses. It is hard to ignore, and hard not to be struck by the contrast once you are aware of it.
Joseph a été aux premières loges de la m: Joseph has had a front-row seat to the transformation of Montréal’s Sud-Ouest neighbourhoods. “I’ve seen the transformation, which I call ‘the disfigurement.’ To me, it’s not good development, it’s disfiguring a neighbourhood,” he says.
Même s’il est loin d’avoir l’âge de ses: Although he is far from the age of his elders, Mr. Jackson could be a dean of Little Burgundy. Before Cantine Burgz, he worked for a long time in the community sector as a community worker. “I did a lot of work with families, with young people,” he notes. He was also a soccer and basketball coach. He left his mark at the Little Burgundy Sports Centre, where he was once involved in management. “I put up posters in the hallway there that talk about all of our heritage,” he says.
Il a fait la même chose au restaurant. «: He did the same thing at the restaurant. “What’s on the walls are people from the community,” he explains, pointing to Oliver Jones and others who have marked history. He doesn’t hesitate to dig into archives and newspaper clippings to recover fragments of the past and of places. “And the restaurant is a nod so we don’t forget our steps. We lived, we told our story. It’s our responsibility to carry it on,” he believes. “If we don’t tell the story, it’s quickly forgotten with gentrification,” he says, before adding that, despite everything, history cannot be erased.
Il regrette le sort réservé à la Petite-: He regrets the fate dealt to Little Burgundy and the erasure of its rich past: “This neighbourhood deserves more attention, deserves to be known. It needs to have a special status.” He dreams of carrying out a project tied to the neighbourhood’s history so that younger generations can learn about it: who lived in the neighbourhood? Why did they live there? And what happened there? For him, one thing is certain: “The ‘Harlem of the North’ is still here!” It is this heritage that he wants to pass on to the communities living there, whether recently arrived or there forever.
Joseph témoigne du fort sentiment d’appa: Joseph speaks of the strong sense of belonging that binds people in the neighbourhood, even those who have just moved in. “One of the things that strikes me is the mutual aid,” he observes.
Il le constate chez les jeunes, avec qui: He sees it among young people, with whom he worked for a long time. “Kids come together in the schoolyard not because of their skin colour or their ethnicity, but because of their identity. That’s a powerful image I have in my head,” he explains. Identity, sometimes, is a neighbourhood that watches them grow up. What does he wish for them now? “Not to do what our generation did, to be able, even very young, to identify certain things and to have a plan for the generation coming up. To have a legacy, to pass on the culture,” says Mr. Joseph. He goes on to stress the work that young people have to do. “We don’t want them to hit walls like we did. We have to prepare the ground, leave them fertile soil.”
S’il est conscient du racisme qui persis: While he is aware of persistent racism and systems of discrimination, Jackson Joseph nevertheless wants to open windows onto opportunities to seize. “You have to roll up your sleeves, get along, create wealth in the community,” he lists. “Me, I try to break down doors. There is a lot of education to be done, even among people who are educated. Some don’t understand the basic principles of mutual aid in a community. There are after-effects of neo-colonialism,” he believes.
Le quartier est l’un des deux grands amo: The neighbourhood is one of Mr. Joseph’s two great loves; the other is Haiti. “I cherish the dream of living there,” he says. And that love, as he puts it so well, no one can take from him.
